On Santaló’s ProblemThanks: This research was supported by the Dr. and Mrs. Milton Leong Fellowships in Science and an ISM Graduate Scholarship.

Abstract.

This paper investigates an isoperimetric-type problem posed by L. A. Santaló, concerning convex surfaces in hyperbolic 3-space that minimize total mean curvature among all convex surfaces with fixed surface area. This problem asks for a characterization of the minimizers and for the optimal form of a Minkowski-type inequality in hyperbolic 3-space. In this work, we propose a conjectural description of the minimizers under certain regularity assumptions. We also construct a new family of convex surfaces as as potential minimizer candidates and establish a property of the singular points of any minimizer.

Key words and phrases: 
Hyperbolic space, Total mean curvature, Minkowski inequality, Convex geometry
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary: 52A40, 53C20; Secondary: 52A38, 53A05.

1. Introduction

This paper concerns an isoperimetric-type problem raised by L. A. Santaló. In 1963, Santaló conjectured [21] (see also [23, p. 78]) that, for any compact convex domain Ω\Omega in hyperbolic space ℍ3​(a)\mathbb{H}^{3}(a) with constant curvature a≤0a\leq 0 and with Γ=∂Ω\Gamma=\partial\Omega,

(1.1) M⁡(Γ)≥16​π​S​(Γ)−4​a​S​(Γ)2,M(\Gamma)\geq\sqrt{16\pi S(\Gamma)-4aS(\Gamma)^{2}},

where S⁡(Γ)S(\Gamma) denotes the surface area of Γ\Gamma, M⁡(Γ):=∫ΓH​𝑑μM(\Gamma):=\int_{\Gamma}Hd\mu is the total mean curvature of Γ\Gamma, and the mean curvature of Γ\Gamma is the trace of the second fundamental form H:=trace​(I​IΓ)H:=\textup{trace}(\mathrm{I\!I}_{\Gamma}). The lower bound of (1.1) would then correspond to the total mean curvature of a sphere with the same area as Γ\Gamma. That is, if (1.1) holds, then geodesic balls minimize total mean curvature among convex surfaces with fixed area.

By scaling the metric, we may take a=−1a=-1 without loss of generality, and thus the ambient space is the standard hyperbolic 33-space ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3}. The conjecture was disproved by Naveira-Solanes [23, p. 815] (see also [20, p. 109] or [10, Note 1.3]). Naveira-Solanes constructed examples indicating that (1.1) is false in general. They showed that a flat double disk, which is isometric to a geodesic sphere in a totally geodesic plane isometric to ℍ2\mathbb{H}^{2}, embedded in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3}, with its two faces counted in the surface area and its edge counted in the singular total mean curvature, gives a counterexample to (1.1) when the surface area S⁡(Γ)S(\Gamma) is large enough. In fact, if we denote M1​(S)M_{1}(S) to be the total mean curvature of the geodesic sphere in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3} with surface area SS, and M2​(S)M_{2}(S) to be the total mean curvature of the flat double disk in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3} with surface area SS, then there exists a constant S^=8​π​(π2−8)16−π2≈7.665\hat{S}=\frac{8\pi(\pi^{2}-8)}{16-\pi^{2}}\approx 7.665 such that M1​(S)>M2​(S)M_{1}(S)>M_{2}(S) whenever S>S^S>\hat{S}. We will explain that this family of convex bodies provides a counterexample to (1.1) in Section 2. On the positive side, Ge-Wang-Wu [8, Theorem 6.1], see also [5], proved that among horo-convex surfaces with fixed surface area, the minimizer of total mean curvature is the geodesic sphere. That is, (1.1) holds for all compact horo-convex surfaces Γ\Gamma in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3}.

In hyperbolic spaces, the total mean curvature of a general convex surface (without any regularity assumption) is well-defined by approximation of outer parallel surfaces, see [10, Section 3]. By Blaschke selection theorem, a minimizer of total mean curvature among convex domains in hyperbolic space ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3} with a given surface area exists. One would like to characterize the geometry of the minimizers, as well as the optimal form of Minkowski-type inequality. We call this Santaló’s problem. This is a generalization of the isoperimetric problem in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3} related to the total mean curvature and surface area.

Minimization of total mean curvature of convex hypersurfaces has long been studied. In 1901, Minkowski [19] proved that the following inequality holds for any non-empty bounded C2C^{2} convex surface Γ⊂ℝ3\Gamma\subset\mathbb{R}^{3},

(1.2) M⁡(Γ)≥16​π​S​(Γ),M(\Gamma)\geq\sqrt{16\pi S(\Gamma)},

and equality holds only when Γ\Gamma is a sphere in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}.

The original proof of Minkowski is based on the isoperimetric inequality together with Steiner-Minkowski formulas. Hence, inequality (1.2) remains true if Γ\Gamma is only a C1,1C^{1,1} surface (or equivalently, if Γ\Gamma has positive reach). If we do not assume any regularity, the same inequality holds if we use the mean width of the convex body enclosed by the surface as an alternative definition for total mean curvature. Guan-Li [13, Theorem 2] proved that (1.2) holds provided that Γ\Gamma is star-shaped and mean-convex. G. Huisken [13, Theorem 6] (see also [17]) showed that (1.2) holds for outward-minimizing surfaces. Dalphin-Henrot-Masnou-Takahashi [6, Theorem 1.1] proved (1.2) in the case where Γ\Gamma is axially symmetric and such that Γ∩P\Gamma\cap P is connected for every affine plane PP orthogonal to the axis of symmetry.

Inequality (1.2) is actually a consequence of a generalization due to Minkowski of the isoperimetric inequality. This generalization uses the notion of mixed volumes and quermassintegrals of convex bodies, and total mean curvature is in fact the first quermassintegral in Euclidean spaces. We refer to [25], [26], [22] for details, and [27] for quermassintegrals in hyperbolic spaces. Generalizations of (1.2) to hyperbolic spaces have been a long-standing problem [21], [7, 20]. Santaló’s problem is one such problem. In recent years, using of curvature flows has led to progress, see [27, 8, 3, 24, 4, 10].

Brendle-Guan-Li [4] proved that for any compact convex body Ω\Omega in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3} with Γ=∂Ω\Gamma=\partial\Omega,

(1.3) W1​(Γ)≥S⁡(Γ)​S⁡(Γ)+4​π+4​π​arcsinh⁡(S⁡(Γ)4​π),W_{1}(\Gamma)\geq\sqrt{S(\Gamma)}\sqrt{S(\Gamma)+4\pi}+4\pi\operatorname{arcsinh}\left(\sqrt{\frac{S(\Gamma)}{4\pi}}\right),

where W1​(Γ)=M⁡(Γ)−2​Vol⁡(Ω)W_{1}(\Gamma)=M(\Gamma)-2\operatorname{Vol}(\Omega) is the first quermassintegral of the convex body Ω\Omega in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3} enclosed by Γ\Gamma, and mean convex means the mean curvature HH is non-negative on Γ\Gamma. Equality holds only if Γ\Gamma is a geodesic sphere in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3}. Although (1.3) is sharp in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3}, the volume of the enclosed domain appears in the inequality. Ghomi-Spruck [10] proved that for any compact convex surface Γ\Gamma in ℍ3​(a)\mathbb{H}^{3}(a) with constant curvature a≤0a\leq 0,

(1.4) M⁡(Γ)≥16​π​S​(Γ)−2​a​S​(Γ)2,M(\Gamma)\geq\sqrt{16\pi S(\Gamma)-2aS(\Gamma)^{2}},

where equality holds only if a=0a=0 and the domain bounded by Γ\Gamma is isometric to a ball in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}. Hence (1.4) is not sharp when the ambient space is fixed to be ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3}. Recently the author [15] strengthened (1.4) to a sharp inequality in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3}. For any compact convex body Ω\Omega in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3} with Γ=∂Ω\Gamma=\partial\Omega,

(1.5) M⁡(Γ)≥16​π​S​(Γ)+2​S​(Γ)2+2​S0​(Vol⁡(Ω))2,M(\Gamma)\geq\sqrt{16\pi S(\Gamma)+2S(\Gamma)^{2}+2S_{0}(\operatorname{Vol}(\Omega))^{2}},

where S0S_{0} denotes the isoperimetric profile function, that is, S0​(x)S_{0}(x) is the surface area of the (geodesic) sphere in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3} with volume xx. Equality holds only if Γ\Gamma is a geodesic sphere in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3}. (1.5) appears to be the sharpest Minkowski-type inequality in hyperbolic 3-space ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3} currently known.

In ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3}, Blaschke selection theorem guarantees the existence of a minimizer of total mean curvature among convex domains with fixed surface area (we include a brief proof in Section 2). Yet, the shape of the general convex minimizer is not known. Therefore, Santaló’s problem, on finding the optimal convex surface with the minimum total mean curvature MM among convex surfaces with fixed surface area SS, is still open. We believe a description of the minimizer and the related geometric inequality can deepen our understanding of hyperbolic geometry, and have applications in mathematical physics and general relativity. For example, the total mean curvature in hyperbolic space is also used in the definition of Wang-Yau’s quasi-local mass in [28, Theorem 1.3].

In the search for the minimizer to Santaló’s problem, the following was observed by Guan [14],

Proposition 1.1.

If Γ\Gamma is a convex surface in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3} that attains the minimum total mean curvature among surfaces with fixed area, that is, there exists a constant S>0S>0 such that

M(Γ)=min{M(Σ):Σ is a convex surface in ℍ3,S(Σ)=S},\displaystyle M(\Gamma)=\min\left\{M(\Sigma):\Sigma\text{ is a convex surface in }\mathbb{H}^{3},S(\Sigma)=S\right\},

then

  1. (1)

    If Γ\Gamma is degenerate, that is, the convex hull of Γ\Gamma has no interior point, then Γ\Gamma is a flat double disk.

  2. (2)

    If Γ\Gamma is C2C^{2} and strictly convex, then Γ\Gamma is a geodesic sphere.

Therefore, if one can prove that every minimizer of Santaló’s problem falls into these two cases, then the minimizer is determined to be either the geodesic sphere or the flat double disk. As a result, Proposition 1.1 led Guan to speculate the optimal inequality for Santaló’s problem to be

(1.6) M⁡(Γ)≥\displaystyle M(\Gamma)\geq min⁡{M1​(S⁡(Γ)),M2​(S⁡(Γ))}\displaystyle\min\left\{M_{1}(S(\Gamma)),M_{2}(S(\Gamma))\right\}
=\displaystyle= min⁡{16​π​S​(Γ)+4​S​(Γ)2,2​π3​S​(Γ)+π24​S​(Γ)2},\displaystyle\min\left\{\sqrt{16\pi S(\Gamma)+4S(\Gamma)^{2}},\sqrt{2\pi^{3}S(\Gamma)+\frac{\pi^{2}}{4}S(\Gamma)^{2}}\right\},

However, it turns out that Santaló’s problem is more complicated. We construct a family of convex bodies in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3} which shows (1.6) does not hold in general.

Theorem 1.2.

There exist positive constants S1,S2S_{1},S_{2} with S1<S2S_{1}<S_{2} such that for any SS with S1<S<S2S_{1}<S<S_{2}, there exists a convex surface ΓS\Gamma^{S} such that ΓS\Gamma^{S} has surface area SS and

M⁡(ΓS)<\displaystyle M(\Gamma^{S})< min⁡{M1​(S),M2​(S)}\displaystyle\min\left\{M_{1}(S),M_{2}(S)\right\}
=\displaystyle= min⁡{16​π​S+4​S2,2​π3​S+π24​S2}.\displaystyle\min\left\{\sqrt{16\pi S+4S^{2}},\sqrt{2\pi^{3}S+\frac{\pi^{2}}{4}S^{2}}\right\}.

We will show that ΓS=Γ⁡(rS,αS)\Gamma^{S}=\Gamma(r_{S},\alpha_{S}) arises from a two-variable family of convex surfaces, and can be described as a geodesic sphere cut by two totally geodesic planes in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3}, forming a "drum" shape. The existence of such surfaces suggests that the optimal convex surface is possibly non-smooth.

In the study of convex bodies without any regularity assumption on their boundaries, the theory of singular points and curvature measures provides useful tools. General convex surfaces may have singular points, where there are multiple unit outer normal vectors (or supporting planes). If the ambient space is 33-dimensional, there are two types of singular points: 11-singular points, with a 22-dimensional normal cone, behaving like edges of a cube; 00-singular points, with a 33-dimensional normal cone, behaving like vertices of a cube. We will give a brief review for singular points and normal cones in Section 2, Subsection 2.4. Regarding the geometry of singular points of minimizers of Santaló’s problem, we will prove the following theorem:

Theorem 1.3.

If Γ\Gamma is a convex surface in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3} that attains the minimal total mean curvature with fixed surface area, then Γ\Gamma has no 00-singular point. That is, for any point pp on Γ\Gamma, the normal cone N⁡(p,conv⁡(Γ))N(p,\operatorname{conv(\Gamma)}) of the convex body conv⁡(Γ)\operatorname{conv}(\Gamma) at pp is 11-dimensional or 22-dimensional; pp is either a 11-singular point or a regular point.

Theorem 1.3 shows that even if the minimizer of Santaló’s problem is non-smooth and singular, it cannot have points that behave like the vertex of a cone or the vertex of a triangular pyramid. This theorem can help to rule out some convex surfaces as minimizers of Santaló’s problem, such as polytopes or cones in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3}.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we list some notations and facts about the known examples, and review the background in convex geometry. In Section 3, we will prove Proposition 1.1. In Section 4, we will construct the new family of convex bodies whose total mean curvature is strictly less than those of the geodesic sphere and the flat double disk with the same area, thereby forming a family of counterexamples to (1.6) and proving Theorem 1.2. In Section 5, we will prove Theorem 1.3 using a local argument based on estimating the total mean curvature of a new convex body truncated by a family of planes at the singular point. We will discuss open questions and further study directions related to Santaló’s problem at the end of this paper.

2. Preliminaries

In this paper, any ambient manifold NN is an (n+1)(n+1)-dimensional space form. A convex set XX in NN is a set whose convex hull conv⁡(X)\operatorname{conv}(X) is itself. A convex hypersurface is the boundary of a convex set. If the ambient manifold NN has dimension dim(N)=3\dim(N)=3, then we call the convex hypersurface a convex surface. A convex body is a bounded closed convex set.

When a hypersurface is C2C^{2}, we have the following equivalent definition for convexity: A convex hypersurface Γ\Gamma of an ambient manifold NN is a closed embedded submanifold of codimension one which, when properly oriented, has positive semidefinite second fundamental form I​IΓ\mathrm{I\!I}_{\Gamma}. A strictly convex hypersurface Γ\Gamma of NN is a convex hypersurface with positive definite second fundamental form.

2.1. Naveira-Solanes’ counterexample

Here we will list some facts about the geometry of hyperbolic 3-space ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3} and examine Naveira-Solanes’ counterexample [20] mentioned above to show that the flat double disks form a counterexample to (1.1). See also [10, Note 1].

For a geodesic sphere 𝕊⁡(r)\mathbb{S}(r) with radius rr in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3}, it is well known that its enclosed volume VV, surface area SS and total mean curvature MM are

V=V⁡(B⁡(r))\displaystyle V=V(B(r)) =2​π​(sinh⁡(r)​cosh⁡(r)−r),\displaystyle=2\pi\left(\sinh(r)\cosh(r)-r\right),
S=S⁡(𝕊⁡(r))\displaystyle S=S(\mathbb{S}(r)) =4πsinh(r)2,\displaystyle=4\pi\sinh(r)^{2},
M=M⁡(𝕊⁡(r))\displaystyle M=M(\mathbb{S}(r)) =8​π​sinh⁡(r)​cosh⁡(r),\displaystyle=8\pi\sinh(r)\cosh(r),

and in particular, we have M=16​π​S+4​S2M=\sqrt{16\pi S+4S^{2}}, and we may denote this function by M1M_{1}, that is,

(2.1) M1​(S):=16​π​S+4​S2.\displaystyle M_{1}(S):=\sqrt{16\pi S+4S^{2}}.

The flat double disk in Naveira-Solanes’ counterexample [20] mentioned above is constructed by taking a disc D⁡(r)D(r) of radius rr in a totally geodesic surface isometric to ℍ2\mathbb{H}^{2} in hyperbolic space ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3}. Its total mean curvature can be computed by taking the limit of the total mean curvature of its outer parallel surface Γ=Γ⁡(r,ϵ)\Gamma=\Gamma(r,\epsilon) at distance ϵ\epsilon. Its surface area consists of two faces of the disk D⁡(r)D(r):

S=2​Sℍ2​(D)=4​π​(cosh⁡(r)−1),S=2S_{\mathbb{H}^{2}}(D)=4\pi(\cosh(r)-1),

where the SS on the left-hand side denotes the total surface area of the flat double disk DD in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3} and the Sℍ2​(D)S_{\mathbb{H}^{2}}(D) denotes the area of the disk with radius rr in ℍ2\mathbb{H}^{2}.

Note that Γ\Gamma consists of a pair of topological disks parallel to DD plus a half tube TT about ∂D\partial D. The mean curvature of the disks vanishes as ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0. On the other hand, S⁡(T)→L⁡(∂D)​π​sinh⁡(ϵ)S(T)\to L(\partial D)\pi\sinh(\epsilon) up to first order (where L⁡(∂D)L(\partial D) denotes the perimeter of ∂D\partial D in ℍ2\mathbb{H}^{2}), since the full tube about ∂D\partial D is foliated by (geodesic) circles of radius ϵ\epsilon. Therefore M⁡(Γ)→∂S⁡(T)/∂ϵ=L⁡(∂D)​π​cosh⁡(ϵ)M(\Gamma)\to\partial S(T)/\partial\epsilon=L(\partial D)\pi\cosh(\epsilon). Thus

M=limϵ→0M⁡(Γ)=L⁡(∂D)​π=2​π2​sinh⁡(r).M=\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}M(\Gamma)=L(\partial D)\pi=2\pi^{2}\sinh(r).

Thus for the flat double disk, its total mean curvature M=M⁡(D⁡(r))M=M(D(r)) and surface area S=S⁡(D⁡(r))S=S(D(r)) satisfies

M=π2​8​π​S+S2=2​π3​S+π24​S2.\displaystyle M=\frac{\pi}{2}\sqrt{8\pi S+S^{2}}=\sqrt{2\pi^{3}S+\frac{\pi^{2}}{4}S^{2}}.

We denote this function by M2M_{2}, that is,

(2.2) M2​(S):=2​π3​S+π24​S2.\displaystyle M_{2}(S):=\sqrt{2\pi^{3}S+\frac{\pi^{2}}{4}S^{2}}.

Clearly when SS is large enough, M2​(S)<M1​(S)M_{2}(S)<M_{1}(S). In fact, M2​(S)<M1​(S)M_{2}(S)<M_{1}(S) for all S>S^=8​π​(π2−8)16−π2≈7.665S>\hat{S}=\frac{8\pi(\pi^{2}-8)}{16-\pi^{2}}\approx 7.665.

In this paper, we will use the Beltrami-Klein model for hyperbolic 3-space. Specifically, we view ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3} as (Bℝ3​(1),gB​K)(B_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}(1),g^{BK}). For x=(x1,x2,x3)∈Bℝ3​(1)⊂ℝ3x=(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})\in B_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}(1)\subset\mathbb{R}^{3}, the Riemannian metric tensor on Tx​ℍ3T_{x}\mathbb{H}^{3} is

gB​K​(x)=11−∑xi2​(∑d​xi⊗d​xi)+1(1−∑xi2)2​((∑xi​d​xi)⊗(∑xi​d​xi)),g^{BK}(x)=\frac{1}{1-\sum x_{i}^{2}}\left(\sum dx_{i}\otimes dx_{i}\right)+\frac{1}{(1-\sum x_{i}^{2})^{2}}\left(\left(\sum x_{i}dx_{i}\right)\otimes\left(\sum x_{i}dx_{i}\right)\right),

where all sums are taken as ∑i=13\sum_{i=1}^{3}.

The following coordinate identity map gives a canonical homeomorphism from ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3} to Bℝ3​(1)B_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}(1).

(2.3) Id:(Bℝ3​(1),gB​K)→\displaystyle\operatorname{Id}:(B_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}(1),g^{BK})\rightarrow (Bℝ3​(1),gℝ3)\displaystyle(B_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}(1),g^{\mathbb{R}^{3}})
(x1,x2,x3)↦\displaystyle(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})\mapsto (x1,x2,x3).\displaystyle(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}).

An advantage of the Beltrami-Klein model is that geodesics are preserved. That is, for a continuous curve γ=γ⁡(t)\gamma=\gamma(t) in ℍ3=(Bℝ3​(1),gB​K)\mathbb{H}^{3}=(B_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}(1),g^{BK}), γ\gamma is a geodesic in (Bℝ3​(1),gB​K)(B_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}(1),g^{BK}) if and only if Id⁡(γ)\operatorname{Id}(\gamma) is a geodesic in (Bℝ3​(1),gℝ3)(B_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}(1),g^{\mathbb{R}^{3}}) (but not necessarily of the same speed).

2.2. Notations and Facts about Geometric Flows

Here we list some evolution equations for geometric flows and recall outer parallel surfaces.

A geometric flow of a C2C^{2} closed hypersurface Γ\Gamma in a Riemannian (n+1)(n+1)-manifold NN [2, 11, 16] is a one-parameter family of immersions X:Γ×[0,T)→NX\colon\Gamma\times[0,T)\to N, Xt​(⋅):=X⁡(⋅,t)X_{t}(\cdot):=X(\cdot,t), given by

(2.4) Xt′​(p)=−Ft​(p)​νt​(p),X0​(p)=p,X_{t}^{\prime}(p)=-F_{t}(p)\nu_{t}(p),\quad\quad\quad X_{0}(p)=p,

where (⋅)′:=∂/∂t⁡(⋅)(\cdot)^{\prime}:=\partial/\partial t(\cdot), νt\nu_{t} is a normal vector field along Γt:=Xt​(Γ)\Gamma_{t}:=X_{t}(\Gamma), and the speed function FtF_{t} is a smooth function on Γt\Gamma_{t}. Let νt​(p)\nu_{t}(p) be the normal and κit​(p)\kappa_{i}^{t}(p) the principal curvatures of Γt\Gamma_{t} at the point Xt​(p)X_{t}(p). Let d​μtd\mu_{t} be the area element induced on Γ\Gamma by XtX_{t}. Gt:=det(I​It)G_{t}:=\det(\mathrm{I\!I}_{t}) and Ht:=trace​(I​It)H_{t}:=\textup{trace}(\mathrm{I\!I}_{t}) are the Gauss-Kronecker curvature and mean curvature of Γt\Gamma_{t}, respectively.

By [16, Thm. 3.2(v)] and [16, Lem. 7.4], for any geometric flow,

(2.5) dd​t​(Ht)\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}(H_{t}) =Δt​Ft+(|I​It|2+Ric⁡(νt))​Ft,\displaystyle=\Delta_{t}F_{t}+\left(|\mathrm{I\!I}_{t}|^{2}+\operatorname{Ric}(\nu_{t})\right)F_{t},
dd​t​(d​μt)\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}(d\mu_{t}) =−Ft​Ht​d​μt,\displaystyle=-F_{t}H_{t}d\mu_{t},
dd​t​S​(Γt)\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}S(\Gamma_{t}) =−∫ΓFtHtdμt,\displaystyle=-\int_{\Gamma}F_{t}H_{t}d\mu_{t},

where |I​It|:=∑(κit)2|\mathrm{I\!I}_{t}|:=\sqrt{\sum(\kappa_{i}^{t})^{2}}, Δt\Delta_{t} is the Laplace-Beltrami operator induced on Γ\Gamma by XtX_{t}, and Ric⁡(νt)\operatorname{Ric}(\nu_{t}) is the Ricci curvature of NN at the point Xt​(p)X_{t}(p) in the direction of νt​(p)\nu_{t}(p), i.e., the sum of sectional curvatures of NN with respect to a pair of orthogonal planes which contain νt​(p)\nu_{t}(p).

In particular, when the speed function Ft≡1F_{t}\equiv 1, the geometric flow exists for all t>0t>0 and is called geodesic normal flow. The hypersurface Γt\Gamma_{t} obtained from Γ\Gamma under geodesic normal flow is called the outer parallel surface of Γ\Gamma at distance tt. An equivalent definition of outer parallel surface is given by Γt:=dΓ^−1​(t)\Gamma_{t}:=\widehat{d_{\Gamma}}^{-1}(t), where dΓ^\widehat{d_{\Gamma}} is the distance function of the convex surface Γ\Gamma, see for example [9, Sec. 2 & 3]. Hence the outer parallel surface is well-defined for any convex surface as an initial surface.

A fact which will be used frequently below is that for any convex surface Γ\Gamma in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3}, its outer parallel surface Γt\Gamma_{t} is C1,1C^{1,1} and convex for any t>0t>0 [9, Sec. 2 & 3]. In particular, for t>0t>0, Γt\Gamma_{t} is twice differentiable almost everywhere and so its total mean curvature M⁡(Γt)M(\Gamma_{t}) is well-defined and positive. We will prove the following invariant along geodesic normal flow:

Proposition 2.1.

Let Γ\Gamma be a convex surface in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3}, and Γt\Gamma_{t} be its outer parallel surface at distance tt. Then for any t≥0t\geq 0,

(2.6) M​(Γt)2−16​π​S​(Γt)−4​S​(Γt)2=M​(Γ)2−16​π​S​(Γ)−4​S​(Γ)2\displaystyle M(\Gamma_{t})^{2}-16\pi S(\Gamma_{t})-4S(\Gamma_{t})^{2}=M(\Gamma)^{2}-16\pi S(\Gamma)-4S(\Gamma)^{2}
Proof.

For any t>0t>0, since Γt\Gamma_{t} is twice differentiable almost everywhere, we may apply (2.5) and plug in Ft≡1F_{t}\equiv 1 to get

dd​t​M​(Γt)=\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}M(\Gamma_{t})= ∫Γ(dd​t​(Ht)​d​μt+Ht​dd​t​(d​μt))\displaystyle\int_{\Gamma}\left(\frac{d}{dt}(H_{t})d\mu_{t}+H_{t}\frac{d}{dt}(d\mu_{t})\right)

2.3. Quermassintegrals of convex bodies in hyperbolic spaces

Here we list definitions and properties of quermassintegrals in Euclidean spaces and hyperbolic spaces. One may refer to [26], [22] and [27] for more background.

For a (geodesically) convex domain KK in a (n+1)(n+1)-dimensional space form NN of constant curvature C∈{−1,0,1}C\in\{-1,0,1\}, an equivalent definition of quermassintegrals is the following:

(2.8) Wk−1​(K):=(n+1−k)ωk−1⋯ω0ωn−1⋯ωn−k​∫ℒk​(N)χ⁡(Lk∩K)​d​Lk​(N),\displaystyle W_{k-1}(K):=\frac{(n+1-k)\omega_{k-1}\cdots\omega_{0}}{\omega_{n-1}\cdots\omega_{n-k}}\int_{\mathcal{L}_{k}(N)}\chi(L_{k}\cap K)dL_{k}(N),
k=1,⋯,n,\displaystyle\quad k=1,\cdots,n,

where ωk\omega_{k} denotes the Lebesgue measure of the kk-dimensional unit sphere 𝕊k\mathbb{S}^{k}. Here ℒk​(N)\mathcal{L}_{k}(N) is the space of kk-dimensional totally geodesic subspaces LkL_{k} in NN and d​Lk​(N)dL_{k}(N) is the natural (invariant) measure on ℒk​(N)\mathcal{L}_{k}(N). The function χ\chi is given by χ⁡(K)=1\chi(K)=1 if K≠∅K\neq\emptyset and χ⁡(∅)=0.\chi(\emptyset)=0. For simplicity, we also use the convention W−1​(K)=V​(K)W_{-1}(K)=V(K) for the volume of KK, and Wn​(K)=ωn−1W_{n}(K)={\omega_{n-1}}. By definition, W0​(K)=S⁡(∂K)W_{0}(K)=S(\partial K).

In Euclidean spaces, if ∂K\partial K is a C2C^{2} hypersurface, the quermassintegrals coincide with the definition in terms of curvature integrals (integral of elementary symmetric functions of curvatures on ∂K\partial K). However, the quermassintegrals and the curvature integrals in hyperbolic spaces or spheres do not coincide. Nevertheless they are closely related. In a space form NN with dimension (n+1)(n+1) and constant curvature C∈{−1,0,1}C\in\{-1,0,1\}, if ∂K\partial K is a C2C^{2} hypersurface, then we have

(2.9) W1​(K)=\displaystyle W_{1}(K)= ∫∂KH​d​μg+n​C​V​(K)=M⁡(∂K)+n​C​V​(K),\displaystyle\int_{\partial K}Hd\mu_{g}+nCV(K)=M(\partial K)+nCV(K),
(2.10) Wk​(K)=\displaystyle W_{k}(K)= ∫∂Kσk​(κ)​d​μg+C⁡(n−k+1)k−1​Wk−2​(K), for ​2≤k≤n,\displaystyle\int_{\partial K}\sigma_{k}(\kappa)d\mu_{g}+\frac{C(n-k+1)}{k-1}W_{k-2}(K),\quad\text{ for }2\leq k\leq n,

Since total mean curvature is also well-defined for general convex bodies (or surfaces) in Cartan-Hadamard spaces without any regularity assumption (see e.g. [10, Section 3]), (2.9) also holds for a general convex body KK.

Combining (2.8) and (2.9), and plugging n=2n=2, k=1k=1, and C=0C=0 or C=−1C=-1 respectively, we have

  • •

    If KK is a convex body in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3}, then

    (2.11) M⁡(∂K)=W1​(K)+2​V​(K)=∫ℒ2​(ℍ3)χ⁡(L2∩K)​d​L2​(ℍ3),\displaystyle M(\partial K)=W_{1}(K)+2V(K)=\int_{\mathcal{L}_{2}(\mathbb{H}^{3})}\chi(L_{2}\cap K)dL_{2}(\mathbb{H}^{3}),
  • •

d​L2​(N)dL_{2}(N) is induced by the action of the isometry group of NN on ℒ2​(N)\mathcal{L}_{2}(N). One may refer to [25, Chapter 4.4] for more details. To estimate total mean curvature using the formulas above, we now give an explicit form of the invariant measure d​L2​(N)dL_{2}(N) for N=ℍ3N=\mathbb{H}^{3} or N=ℝ3N=\mathbb{R}^{3}. After taking an origin OO in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}, we may parameterize ℒ2​(ℝ3)\mathcal{L}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3}) as follows:

ℒ2(ℝ3)={Plane(ν,R):ν∈𝕊2,R>0},\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3})=\left\{\operatorname{Plane}(\nu,R):\nu\in\mathbb{S}^{2},R>0\right\},

where Plane⁡(ν,R)\operatorname{Plane}(\nu,R) is the plane in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} with unit outer normal ν\nu, and the distance from Plane⁡(ν,R)\operatorname{Plane}(\nu,R) to OO is RR, or more precisely,

(2.13) Plane⁡(ν,R):={p∈ℝ3:⟨p,ν⟩=R},\displaystyle\operatorname{Plane}(\nu,R):=\left\{p\in\mathbb{R}^{3}:\left\langle p,\nu\right\rangle=R\right\},

ℒ2(ℍ3)={Plane(ν,R):ν∈𝕊2,R>0},\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{2}(\mathbb{H}^{3})=\left\{\operatorname{Plane}(\nu,R):\nu\in\mathbb{S}^{2},R>0\right\},

where Plane⁡(ν,R)\operatorname{Plane}(\nu,R) is a plane (totally geodesic 22-dimensional submanifold) in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3} that that is analogous to its counterpart in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}. In the Beltrami-Klein model where the origin is taken as the same origin OO, we may formulate it as:

where Id\operatorname{Id} is the Beltrami-Klein identity map given by (2.3), and the Plane⁡(ν,tanh⁡(R))\operatorname{Plane}(\nu,\tanh(R)) on the right-hand side is a plane in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} defined in (2.13). Note that the distance between the hyperbolic plane Plane⁡(ν,R)\operatorname{Plane}(\nu,R) defined in (2.15) and the origin OO is still RR. Under this parametrization, the invariant measure can be formulated as

(2.16) d​L2​(ℍ3)=2​(1+2​sinh2⁡(R))​d​R∧d​μ𝕊2​(ν).\displaystyle dL_{2}(\mathbb{H}^{3})=2(1+2\sinh^{2}(R))dR\wedge d\mu_{\mathbb{S}^{2}}(\nu).

2.4. Convexity and Normal Cones

Here we review the definitions and facts about the normal cone and singular (regular) points, together with basics about curvature measures used in convex geometry. One may refer to [25] for definitions and facts in Euclidean spaces. The counterparts in space forms are similar.

A supporting hyperplane PP of a closed set XX is a totally geodesic hypersurface in NN such that XX is entirely contained in one of the two closed half-spaces bounded by the hyperplane PP, and P∩∂X≠∅P\cap\partial X\neq\emptyset. We say that PP is a supporting hyperplane of XX at pp, if PP is supporting hyperplane of XX, and p∈P∩∂Xp\in P\cap\partial X. If the ambient manifold NN has dimension dim(N)=3\dim(N)=3, then we call the supporting hyperplane a supporting plane.

If KK is a convex body, and p∈∂Kp\in\partial K, then clearly there exists a supporting hyperplane PP of KK at pp. The supporting hyperplane at a point pp may not be unique. The set of all supporting hyperplanes at p∈∂Kp\in\partial K with respect to the convex body KK is denoted by Supp⁡(p,K)\operatorname{Supp}(p,K).

Conversely, if KK is a closed set with non-empty interior such that every point pp on the boundary has a supporting hyperplane PP, then KK is a convex body and KK is the intersection of all its supporting closed half-spaces (namely the half-space bounded by P=P⁡(p)P=P(p) that contains K). XX is a strictly convex set if every supporting hyperplane of XX intersects XX at only a single point.

In the following context of this subsection, we take the ambient manifold NN to be the hyperbolic 3-space ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3}.

If Supp⁡(p,K)\operatorname{Supp}(p,K) consists of only one element (one plane), we say pp is a regular point of the convex surface ∂K\partial K. In this case, there exists a unique supporting plane of p∈∂Kp\in\partial K with respect to KK. Otherwise, we say pp is a singular point of ∂K\partial K. See [25, Chapter 2.2]. If pp is singular, let r=r⁡(p)r=r(p) be the maximum number of linearly independent supporting planes at pp with respect to KK. Since dim(Tp​ℍ3)=3\dim(T_{p}\mathbb{H}^{3})=3, we know r=2r=2 or r=3r=3. We call pp a (3−r)(3-r)-singular point.

We denote the set of regular points on ∂K\partial K by Reg⁡(∂K)\operatorname{Reg}(\partial K). For s=0,1s=0,1, we denote the set of ss-singular points on ∂K\partial K by Sings⁡(∂K)\operatorname{Sing}^{s}(\partial K).

If KK is a convex body in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3}, for any p∈∂Kp\in\partial K and any supporting plane P∈Supp⁡(p,K)P\in\operatorname{Supp}(p,K), PP can be determined by its non-zero normal vector ν⁡(p,H)∈Tp​ℍ3\nu(p,H)\in T_{p}\mathbb{H}^{3}, that is, ν⁡(p,H)\nu(p,H) is the unique unit vector up to orientation such that

P={expp(v):v∈Tpℍ3,g¯(v,ν(p,H))=0 in Tpℍ3},\displaystyle P=\left\{\exp_{p}(v):v\in T_{p}\mathbb{H}^{3},\bar{g}\left(v,\nu(p,H)\right)=0\text{ in }T_{p}\mathbb{H}^{3}\right\},

where g¯\bar{g} is the Riemannian metric of ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3}. We take such a vector ν\nu to be outward with respect to KK, that is, expp⁡(t​ν)\exp_{p}(t\nu) lies in ℍ3\K\mathbb{H}^{3}\backslash K for any t>0t>0.

We define the normal cone N⁡(p,K)N(p,K) of p∈∂Kp\in\partial K with respect to the convex body KK as the set of outer normal vectors (not necessarily unit vectors) of all supporting planes of pp with respect to KK. That is,

(2.17) N(p,K)={O}∪{λν(p,H):λ>0,H∈Supp(p,K)}⊂Tpℍ3.\displaystyle N(p,K)=\{O\}\cup\left\{\lambda\nu(p,H):\lambda>0,H\in\operatorname{Supp}(p,K)\right\}\subset T_{p}\mathbb{H}^{3}.

Note that the vectors in a normal cone are not necessarily unit vectors. We denote the set of unit normal vectors at a point p∈∂Kp\in\partial K by 𝒩⁡(p,K)\mathcal{N}(p,K), that is,

𝒩⁡(p,K):={ν∈N⁡(p,K):‖ν‖=1}.\displaystyle\mathcal{N}(p,K):=\left\{\nu\in N(p,K):\|\nu\|=1\right\}.

The unit normal bundle 𝒩⁡(K)\mathcal{N}(K) is defined by 𝒩⁡(K):=⋃p∈∂K𝒩⁡(p,K)\mathcal{N}(K):=\bigcup_{p\in\partial K}\mathcal{N}(p,K). In this paper, we will also use the notation relint⁡𝒩⁡(p,K)\operatorname{relint}\mathcal{N}(p,K), which means the relative interior of 𝒩⁡(p,K)\mathcal{N}(p,K) in its affine hull in {ν∈Tp​ℍ3:‖ν‖=1}\{\nu\in T_{p}\mathbb{H}^{3}:\|\nu\|=1\}, which is isometric to 𝕊2\mathbb{S}^{2}.

Claim.

N⁡(p,K)N(p,K) is a convex cone in (Tp​ℍ3,g¯)(T_{p}\mathbb{H}^{3},\bar{g}), where g¯\bar{g} denotes the Riemannian metric in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3}.

Proof of the Claim.

It suffices to prove that for any non-zero vectors ν1,ν2∈N⁡(p,K)\nu_{1},\nu_{2}\in N(p,K), and any λ∈(0,1)\lambda\in(0,1), λ​ν1+(1−λ)​ν2∈N⁡(p,K)\lambda\nu_{1}+(1-\lambda)\nu_{2}\in N(p,K). If λ​ν1+(1−λ)​ν2=0\lambda\nu_{1}+(1-\lambda)\nu_{2}=0, the claim follows directly. Hence we assume λ​ν1+(1−λ)​ν2≠0\lambda\nu_{1}+(1-\lambda)\nu_{2}\neq 0 in the following proof.

Clearly if HH is a supporting plane of KK in ℍ3=(Bℝ3​(1),gB​K)\mathbb{H}^{3}=(B_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}(1),g^{BK}), then after being mapped into Bℝ3​(1)⊂ℝ3B_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}(1)\subset\mathbb{R}^{3} as in (2.3), Id⁡(H)\operatorname{Id}(H) is a supporting plane of Id⁡(K)\operatorname{Id}(K) in (Bℝ3​(1),gℝ3)(B_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}(1),g^{\mathbb{R}^{3}}), where we choose the Beltrami-Klein model so that Id⁡(p)\operatorname{Id}(p) is the origin in (Bℝ3​(1),gℝ3)(B_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}(1),g^{\mathbb{R}^{3}}). Moreover, Id⁡(K)\operatorname{Id}(K) is also a convex body in (Bℝ3​(1),gℝ3)(B_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}(1),g^{\mathbb{R}^{3}}).

By definition, there exist two totally geodesic planes H1,H2H_{1},H_{2} in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3} such that ν1=ν⁡(p,H1),ν2=ν⁡(p,H2)\nu_{1}=\nu(p,H_{1}),\nu_{2}=\nu(p,H_{2}). Consider Id⁡(H1)\operatorname{Id}(H_{1}) and Id⁡(H2)\operatorname{Id}(H_{2}) as planes in (Bℝ3​(1),gℝ3)(B_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}(1),g^{\mathbb{R}^{3}}) passing through the origin. Consider H¯3=λ​Id⁡(H1)+(1−λ)​Id⁡(H2)\overline{H}_{3}=\lambda\operatorname{Id}(H_{1})+(1-\lambda)\operatorname{Id}(H_{2}). Since Id⁡(K)\operatorname{Id}(K) is convex, and both Id⁡(H1)\operatorname{Id}(H_{1}) and Id⁡(H2)\operatorname{Id}(H_{2}) support Id⁡(K)\operatorname{Id}(K), H¯3\overline{H}_{3} is also a supporting plane of Id⁡(K)\operatorname{Id}(K), hence H3:=Id−1⁡(H3¯)H_{3}:=\operatorname{Id}^{-1}(\overline{H_{3}}) is a supporting plane of KK.

Since ν⁡(p,H3)=1‖λ​ν1+(1−λ)​ν2‖​(λ​ν1+(1−λ)​ν2)\nu(p,H_{3})=\frac{1}{\|\lambda\nu_{1}+(1-\lambda)\nu_{2}\|}\left(\lambda\nu_{1}+(1-\lambda)\nu_{2}\right), we have λ​ν1+(1−λ)​ν2∈N⁡(p,K)\lambda\nu_{1}+(1-\lambda)\nu_{2}\in N(p,K). ∎

If pp is regular, then N⁡(p,K)N(p,K) is 11-dimensional. In this case, there exists a unique unit outer normal vector in Tp​ℍ3T_{p}\mathbb{H}^{3} at pp. Otherwise, if pp is singular, then N⁡(p,K)N(p,K) is at least 22-dimensional. Since dim(Tp​ℍ3)=3\dim(T_{p}\mathbb{H}^{3})=3, we know if pp is singular, then dimN⁡(p,K)=2\dim N(p,K)=2 or dimN⁡(p,K)=3\dim N(p,K)=3. If pp is a 00-singular point, then dimN⁡(p,K)=3\dim N(p,K)=3. If pp is a 11-singular point, then dimN⁡(p,K)=2\dim N(p,K)=2.

3. Proof of Proposition 1.1: Minimizers under special conditions

In this section, we will first prove the existence of a minimizer in Santaló’s problem. Then we will prove Proposition 1.1, that is, the classification of minimizers in two cases: degenerate case and C2C^{2} strictly convex case. The proofs of Proposition 1.1 follow from Guan [14].

3.1. Existence of a minimizer

For any fixed real number S0∈(0,∞)S_{0}\in(0,\infty), consider the set of convex bodies defined by 𝒦3​(S0)={K∈𝒦3​(ℍ3):∂K​ has surface area ​S0}\mathcal{K}^{3}(S_{0})=\left\{K\in\mathcal{K}^{3}(\mathbb{H}^{3}):\partial K\text{ has surface area }S_{0}\right\}, where 𝒦3​(ℍ3)\mathcal{K}^{3}(\mathbb{H}^{3}) denotes the set of all convex bodies in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3}. By Ghomi-Spruck [10], for any convex surface Γ\Gamma in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3}, we have

M⁡(Γ)≥16​π​S​(Γ)+2​S​(Γ)2,M(\Gamma)\geq\sqrt{16\pi S(\Gamma)+2S(\Gamma)^{2}},

hence we know for any K∈𝒦3​(S0)K\in\mathcal{K}^{3}(S_{0}), M⁡(∂K)≥16​π​S0+2​S02,M(\partial K)\geq\sqrt{16\pi S_{0}+2S_{0}^{2}}, thus

inf{M⁡(∂K):K∈𝒦3​(S0)}≥16​π​S0+2​S02>0.\inf\left\{M(\partial K):K\in\mathcal{K}^{3}(S_{0})\right\}\geq\sqrt{16\pi S_{0}+2S_{0}^{2}}>0.

We denote M0:=inf{M⁡(∂K):K∈𝒦3​(S0)}M_{0}:=\inf\left\{M(\partial K):K\in\mathcal{K}^{3}(S_{0})\right\}. Consider a sequence of convex bodies KnK_{n} such that limn→∞M⁡(∂Kn)=M0\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}M(\partial K_{n})=M_{0}. We denote Γn:=∂Kn\Gamma_{n}:=\partial K_{n}. Without loss of generality, we assume M⁡(Γn)≤M0+1M(\Gamma_{n})\leq M_{0}+1 for all nn.

By the inequality relating diameter and total mean curvature in hyperbolic space [30], there exists a constant CC such that for any convex closed connected embedded surface Γ\Gamma in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3},

diam⁡(Γ)≤C​∫ΓH​𝑑μ,\operatorname{diam}(\Gamma)\leq C\int_{\Gamma}Hd\mu,

where diam⁡(⋅)\operatorname{diam}(\cdot) denotes the diameter of a set in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3}. Hence for all nn, since ∂Kn\partial K_{n} are convex surfaces,

diam⁡(Kn)=diam⁡(Γn)≤C​∫ΓnH​𝑑μ=C⋅M⁡(Γn)≤C⁡(M0+1).\operatorname{diam}(K_{n})=\operatorname{diam}(\Gamma_{n})\leq C\int_{\Gamma_{n}}Hd\mu=C\cdot M(\Gamma_{n})\leq C(M_{0}+1).

Therefore by applying isometric translations to these convex bodies appropriately, we may assume for all nn, KnK_{n} is contained in the geodesic ball B⁡(C⁡(M0+1))B(C(M_{0}+1)) with radius C⁡(M0+1)C(M_{0}+1) in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3}.

By Blaschke Selection Theorem in metric spaces, see for example [12], any bounded sequence of convex bodies in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3} contains a convergent subsequence with respect to the Hausdorff metric. Hence there exists a convex body K∞K_{\infty} and a sequence mn→∞m_{n}\rightarrow\infty, such that KmnK_{m_{n}} tends to K∞K_{\infty} with respect to Hausdorff metric.

Hence S0=limn→∞S⁡(∂Kmn)=S⁡(∂K∞)S_{0}=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}S(\partial K_{m_{n}})=S(\partial K_{\infty}), and M0=limn→∞M⁡(∂Kmn)=M⁡(∂K∞)M_{0}=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}M(\partial K_{m_{n}})=M(\partial K_{\infty}), that is, K∞∈𝒦3​(S0)K_{\infty}\in\mathcal{K}^{3}(S_{0}), and M⁡(∂K∞)=inf{M⁡(∂K):K∈𝒦3​(S0)}.M(\partial K_{\infty})=\inf\left\{M(\partial K):K\in\mathcal{K}^{3}(S_{0})\right\}. That is, ∂K∞\partial K_{\infty} is the minimizer of total mean curvature of convex surfaces with surface area S0S_{0}.

3.2. Degenerate minimizer

Proof of Proposition 1.1(1).

If Γ\Gamma is degenerate, then by convexity, Γ\Gamma is a subset of a totally geodesic submanifold isometric to ℍ2\mathbb{H}^{2} in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3}, with its two faces counted into surface area, and its edge counted into singular mean curvature.

Denote this convex body in ℍ2\mathbb{H}^{2} by K1K_{1}. Then we have

S⁡(Γ)=2​S​(K1),M⁡(Γ)=π​L​(∂K1),\displaystyle S(\Gamma)=2S(K_{1}),\quad M(\Gamma)=\pi L(\partial K_{1}),

where S⁡(K1)S(K_{1}) and L⁡(∂K1)L(\partial K_{1}) denote area of K1K_{1} and perimeter of ∂K1\partial K_{1} in ℍ2\mathbb{H}^{2}, respectively. Then Santaló’s problem in this case is equivalent to the isoperimetric problem in ℍ2\mathbb{H}^{2}. By [29], the convex body in ℍ2\mathbb{H}^{2} that minimizes perimeter with fixed area is the geodesic ball in ℍ2\mathbb{H}^{2}. Hence Γ\Gamma is the flat double disk in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3}. ∎

3.3. C2C^{2} strictly convex minimizer

Fix the surface area SS. If a convex surface Γ\Gamma is the minimizer of total mean curvature, and a piece of Γ\Gamma is C2C^{2} and strictly convex, that is, both of its principal curvatures are positive in an open subset UU of Γ\Gamma, then we may apply the method of Lagrange multipliers to derive the Euler-Lagrange equation of the surface. Given any normal variation of the surface Γ\Gamma by a geometric flow, say ∂tΓt=ft​νt\partial_{t}\Gamma_{t}=f_{t}\nu_{t}, with Γ0=Γ\Gamma_{0}=\Gamma and f0=ff_{0}=f, where ff is a function on Γ\Gamma compactly supported in UU which is a relatively open subset of Γ\Gamma, we have at time t=0t=0, the first variation of total mean curvature and area are given by

∂tM=∫U2​(G+1)​f​𝑑μ,\displaystyle\partial_{t}M=\int_{U}2(G+1)fd\mu,
∂tS=∫UH​f​𝑑μ.\displaystyle\partial_{t}S=\int_{U}Hfd\mu.

One may refer to Section 3, Subsection 2.2 for details.

Since both principal curvatures of Γ\Gamma are positive in UU, there exists ϵ>0\epsilon>0 such that for any tt with −ϵ<t<ϵ-\epsilon<t<\epsilon, Γt\Gamma_{t} is still a C2C^{2} strictly convex surface in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3}.

Therefore, as a critical point of the functional MM, Γ\Gamma satisfies the Euler-Lagrange equation

By convexity, λ\lambda is positive. If the whole surface of the minimizer Γ\Gamma is C2C^{2} and strictly convex, the equation above holds globally on Γ\Gamma.

Proof of Proposition 1.1(2).

4. Proof of Theorem 1.2: A new family of convex surfaces

In this subsection, we will construct a two-variable family of convex surfaces Γ⁡(r,α)\Gamma(r,\alpha) that forms a counterexample to (1.6) and thereby proves Theorem 1.2. We construct Γ⁡(r,α)\Gamma(r,\alpha) as follows. Id−1((x1,x2,x3)∈Bℝ3(1):(x1)2+(x2)2+(x3)2≤r^2,−r^cos(α)≤x3≤r^cos(α)),\displaystyle\operatorname{Id}^{-1}\left((x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})\in B_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}(1):(x_{1})^{2}+(x_{2})^{2}+(x_{3})^{2}\leq\hat{r}^{2},-\hat{r}\cos(\alpha)\leq x_{3}\leq\hat{r}\cos(\alpha)\right),

where the identity map is defined in (2.3), and r^=tanh⁡(r)\hat{r}=\tanh(r) is the Euclidean radius of the image under Id\operatorname{Id} of the sphere 𝕊⁡(r)\mathbb{S}(r) in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3} with radius rr. See also Figure 1.

We denote the following three points by O:=Id−1⁡(0,0,0)O:=\operatorname{Id}^{-1}(0,0,0), A:=Id−1⁡(0,0,r^​cos⁡(α))A:=\operatorname{Id}^{-1}(0,0,\hat{r}\cos(\alpha)) and B:=Id−1⁡(r^​sin⁡(α),0,r^​cos⁡(α))B:=\operatorname{Id}^{-1}(\hat{r}\sin(\alpha),0,\hat{r}\cos(\alpha)). In the hyperbolic right triangle O​A​BOAB (as shown in Figure 1), we will introduce the following notation. Clearly by definition of Ω⁡(r,α)\Omega(r,\alpha), we have the hypotenuse distℍ3⁡(O,B)=r=arctanh⁡(r^)\operatorname{dist}_{\mathbb{H}^{3}}(O,B)=r=\operatorname{arctanh}(\hat{r}), and the angle ∠​A​O​B=α\angle AOB=\alpha. By the hyperbolic law of cosines, the angle β:=∠​A​B​O\beta:=\angle ABO is given by cot⁡(β)​cot⁡(α)=cosh⁡(r)\cot(\beta)\cot(\alpha)=\cosh(r).

We decompose the surface Γ⁡(r,α)\Gamma(r,\alpha) into three pairwise disjoint subsets. Namely Γ⁡(r,α)=Γ1​(r,α)∪Γ2​(r,α)∪Γ3​(r,α)\Gamma(r,\alpha)=\Gamma_{1}(r,\alpha)\cup\Gamma_{2}(r,\alpha)\cup\Gamma_{3}(r,\alpha), where

Γ1​(r,α):=\displaystyle\Gamma_{1}(r,\alpha):=
Id−1{(x1,x2,x3)∈Bℝ3(1):0≤(x1)2+(x2)2≤r^2,\displaystyle\operatorname{Id}^{-1}\left\{(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})\in B_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}(1):0\leq(x_{1})^{2}+(x_{2})^{2}\leq\hat{r}^{2},\right.
x3=r^cos(α) or −r^cos(α)}\displaystyle\left.x_{3}=\hat{r}\cos(\alpha)\text{ or }-\hat{r}\cos(\alpha)\right\}

denotes the upper and lower "flat" parts, which are isometric to two identical disjoint disks embedded in ℍ2\mathbb{H}^{2} with radius r1r_{1};

Γ2​(r,α):=\displaystyle\Gamma_{2}(r,\alpha):=
Id−1{(x1,x2,x3)∈Bℝ3(1):(x1)2+(x2)2+(x3)2=r^2,\displaystyle\operatorname{Id}^{-1}\left\{(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})\in B_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}(1):(x_{1})^{2}+(x_{2})^{2}+(x_{3})^{2}=\hat{r}^{2},\right.

The solid angle of the spherical part Γ2​(r,α)\Gamma_{2}(r,\alpha) in 𝕊2​(r)\mathbb{S}^{2}(r) is 4​π−2⋅2​π​(1−cos⁡(α))=4​π​cos⁡(α)4\pi-2\cdot 2\pi(1-\cos(\alpha))=4\pi\cos(\alpha), hence its area proportion of the whole sphere 𝕊2​(r)\mathbb{S}^{2}(r) is cos⁡(α)\cos(\alpha);

5. Proof of Theorem 1.3: Singularity property

In this section, we will prove Theorem 1.3. One may refer to Section 2 for definitions and facts about singular points, and integral geometric formulas for quermassintegrals.

We will use a local argument. The idea is that if there exists a 00-singular point on the minimizer surface Γ\Gamma, then it forms a "vertex" of the whole convex body Ω=conv⁡(Γ)\Omega=\operatorname{conv}(\Gamma). Hence we can shrink Ω\Omega infinitesimally by truncating it with a family of planes at the "vertex". After the infinitesimal shrinking, we will then perform an infinitesimal expansion using outward geodesic normal flow (outer parallel surface) to restore the area. Finally, we construct a convex surface Γ′\Gamma^{\prime} with the same area as Γ\Gamma, and we will prove Γ′\Gamma^{\prime} has strictly less total mean curvature than Γ\Gamma, which contradicts the assumption that Γ\Gamma is a minimizer. In the whole proof, we will use the Beltrami-Klein model to describe the infinitesimal shrinking in Euclidean space.

Proof of Theorem 1.3.

Let Γ\Gamma be a minimizer to Santaló’s problem. Let Ω=conv⁡(Γ)\Omega=\operatorname{conv}(\Gamma).

If Γ\Gamma is degenerate, then by Proposition 1.1(1), it is a flat double disk, whose two open disks are regular points, and the points along the circular edge are 11-singular points. Hence the theorem follows. In what follows, we will assume Γ\Gamma is non-degenerate, that is, its convex hull has non-empty interior.

Suppose that there exists a 00-singular point pp on Γ\Gamma. Then the normal cone N⁡(p,Ω)N(p,\Omega) has at least three linearly independent unit vectors. We choose P1,P2,P3∈Supp⁡(p,Ω)P_{1},P_{2},P_{3}\in\operatorname{Supp}(p,\Omega) to be three linearly independent supporting planes of Ω\Omega at pp. Let U1U_{1} be the closed half-space of ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3} divided by P1P_{1} that contains Ω\Omega, and define U2U_{2}, U3U_{3} similarly for P2P_{2}, P3P_{3}, respectively. Since P1P_{1}, P2P_{2} and P3P_{3} are linearly independent, Ω1:=U1∩U2∩U3\Omega_{1}:=U_{1}\cap U_{2}\cap U_{3} is a closed unbounded triangular pyramid, and Ω⊂Ω1\Omega\subset\Omega_{1}. We denote Γ1:=∂Ω1\Gamma_{1}:=\partial\Omega_{1}.

For any unit normal vector ν∈relint⁡𝒩⁡(p,Ω)\nu\in\operatorname{relint}{\mathcal{N}(p,\Omega)} (where relint⁡𝒩⁡(p,Ω)\operatorname{relint}\mathcal{N}(p,\Omega) means the relative interior of 𝒩⁡(p,Ω)\mathcal{N}(p,\Omega) in its affine hull in {ν∈Tp​ℍ3:‖ν‖=1}\{\nu\in T_{p}\mathbb{H}^{3}:\|\nu\|=1\}, as stated in Section 2, Subsection 2.4), we define p⁡(ν,d)p(\nu,d) to be the point expp⁡(−d​ν)\exp_{p}(-d\nu), and define ν⁡(d)\nu(d) to be the image of ν\nu parallel transported from Tp​ℍ3T_{p}\mathbb{H}^{3} to Tp⁡(ν,d)​ℍ3T_{p(\nu,d)}\mathbb{H}^{3} for d>0d>0, and P⁡(ν,d)P(\nu,d) to be the parallel-transported hyperbolic plane. That is,

P(ν,d):={expp⁡(ν,d)(v):v∈Tp⁡(ν,d)ℍ3,g¯(v,ν(d))=0 in Tp⁡(ν,d)ℍ3}.\displaystyle P(\nu,d):=\left\{\exp_{p(\nu,d)}(v):v\in T_{p(\nu,d)}\mathbb{H}^{3},\bar{g}\left(v,\nu(d)\right)=0\text{ in }T_{p(\nu,d)}\mathbb{H}^{3}\right\}.

Clearly the distance from pp to P⁡(ν,d)P(\nu,d) is dd in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3}.

For any unit normal vector ν\nu in relint⁡𝒩⁡(p,Ω)\operatorname{relint}{\mathcal{N}(p,\Omega)}, and for d>0d>0 small enough, Ω\Omega and Ω1\Omega_{1} will both be divided by P⁡(ν,d)P(\nu,d) into two convex subsets. The proof will focus on the infinitesimal change of surface area and total mean curvature of the truncated convex surface. The specific choice of ν∈relint⁡𝒩⁡(p,Ω)\nu\in\operatorname{relint}{\mathcal{N}(p,\Omega)} used to perform this cut is to be determined later, and we will set up the notations and lemmas first.

Plane⁡(B𝕊2​(−Id⋆⁡ν,δ)×(−c2​d,0))⊂ℒ~,\operatorname{Plane}\left(B_{\mathbb{S}^{2}}(-\operatorname{Id}_{\star}\nu,\delta)\times(-c_{2}d,0)\right)\subset\widetilde{\mathcal{L}},

which proves (5.6), and thus (5.3) follows.

Now we will use (5.3) in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} to prove (5.1) in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3}. Since for any point q∈(Bℝ3​(1),gB​K)=ℍ3q\in(B_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}(1),g^{BK})=\mathbb{H}^{3}, OPENdistℝ3⁡(Id⁡(O),Id⁡(q))=tanh⁡(distℍ3⁡(O,q)))\operatorname{dist}_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}(\operatorname{Id}(O),\operatorname{Id}(q))=\tanh\left(\operatorname{dist}_{\mathbb{H}^{3}}(O,q))\right), we have

(5.8) ℒ~=Id(ℒ)={Plane(τ,tanh(R)):τ∈𝕊2,R>0, such that Plane(τ,R)∈ℒ.}.\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}=\operatorname{Id}(\mathcal{L})=\left\{\operatorname{Plane}(\tau,\tanh(R)):\tau\in\mathbb{S}^{2},R>0,\text{ such that }\operatorname{Plane}(\tau,R)\in\mathcal{L}.\right\}.

By (2.16), we know

(5.9) d​L2​(ℍ3)=2​(1+2​sinh2⁡(R))​d​R∧d​μ𝕊2.\displaystyle dL_{2}(\mathbb{H}^{3})=2(1+2\sinh^{2}(R))dR\wedge d\mu_{\mathbb{S}^{2}}.

Combining (5.8) and (5.9), since sinh⁡(R)/R→1\sinh(R)/R\to 1 and tanh⁡(R)/R→1\tanh(R)/R\to 1 as R→0R\to 0, if dd is small enough, there exist constants cc and c1c_{1} such that

d​L2​(ℍ3)​(ℒ)>c⋅d​L2​(ℝ3)​(Id⁡(ℒ))>c1​d,\displaystyle dL_{2}(\mathbb{H}^{3})(\mathcal{L})>c\cdot dL_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3})(\operatorname{Id}(\mathcal{L}))>c_{1}d,

hence (5.2) follows, which proves (5.1). ∎

We now combine the two lemmas to finish the proof. By Lemma 5.1 and Lemma 5.2, we choose any ν∈𝒩⁡(p,Ω1)⊂𝒩⁡(p,Ω)\nu\in\mathcal{N}(p,\Omega_{1})\subset\mathcal{N}(p,\Omega). As d→0+d\to 0^{+}, there exists positive constants cc and CC, depending only on Ω,p,ν\Omega,p,\nu, such that

(5.10) M⁡(Γ)−M⁡(Γ−​(ν,d))>c​d,\displaystyle M(\Gamma)-M(\Gamma^{-}(\nu,d))>cd,
(5.11) S⁡(Γ)−S⁡(Γ−​(ν,d))≤C​d2.\displaystyle S(\Gamma)-S(\Gamma^{-}(\nu,d))\leq Cd^{2}.

We now apply geodesic normal flow to Γ−​(ν,d)\Gamma^{-}(\nu,d). From the proof of Proposition 2.1, there exists a constant T>0T>0 such that the outer parallel surface XT​(Γ−​(ν,d))X_{T}(\Gamma^{-}(\nu,d)) at distance TT has the same surface area as Γ\Gamma. Denote it by Γ′\Gamma^{\prime}. Then S⁡(Γ′)=S⁡(Γ)S(\Gamma^{\prime})=S(\Gamma).

By Proposition 2.1 we have

M​(Γ′)2−16​π​S​(Γ′)−4​S​(Γ′)2=M​(Γ−​(ν,d))2−16​π​S​(Γ−​(ν,d))−4​S​(Γ−​(ν,d))2,M(\Gamma^{\prime})^{2}-16\pi S(\Gamma^{\prime})-4S(\Gamma^{\prime})^{2}=M(\Gamma^{-}(\nu,d))^{2}-16\pi S(\Gamma^{-}(\nu,d))-4S(\Gamma^{-}(\nu,d))^{2},

Hence,

M​(Γ′)2−M​(Γ)2\displaystyle M(\Gamma^{\prime})^{2}-M(\Gamma)^{2}
=\displaystyle= M​(Γ−​(ν,d))2−M​(Γ)2−16​π​[S⁡(Γ−​(ν,d))−S⁡(Γ)]\displaystyle M(\Gamma^{-}(\nu,d))^{2}-M(\Gamma)^{2}-16\pi\left[S(\Gamma^{-}(\nu,d))-S(\Gamma)\right]
−4​[S​(Γ−​(ν,d))2−S​(Γ)2].\displaystyle-4\left[S(\Gamma^{-}(\nu,d))^{2}-S(\Gamma)^{2}\right].

Substituting (5.10) and (5.11), we obtain

M​(Γ′)2−M​(Γ)2<−[M⁡(Γ−​(ν,d))+M⁡(Γ)]​c​d+C​d2≤−c0​d+C​d2M(\Gamma^{\prime})^{2}-M(\Gamma)^{2}<-\left[M(\Gamma^{-}(\nu,d))+M(\Gamma)\right]cd+Cd^{2}\leq-c_{0}d+Cd^{2}

for constants c0,Cc_{0},C depending only on Ω\Omega, pp and ν\nu. Therefore, for dd small enough, S⁡(Γ′)=S⁡(Γ)S(\Gamma^{\prime})=S(\Gamma) but M⁡(Γ′)<M⁡(Γ)M(\Gamma^{\prime})<M(\Gamma), so Γ\Gamma is not a minimizer, which contradicts the assumption. Hence if Γ\Gamma is a convex minimizer, then Γ\Gamma has no 00-singular point. ∎

Remark 5.4.

Open Questions. Some further study directions to Santaló’s problem will be listed here. Clearly, the question of greatest interest is:

Question 5.5.

What is the shape of a minimizer to Santaló’s problem, that is, of a convex surface in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3} that minimizes total mean curvature among convex surfaces with fixed area?

The explicit form of the minimizer may be difficult to find; however, we may ask the following related questions to understand its geometry:

Question 5.6.

Let Γ\Gamma be a minimizer to Santaló’s problem then

  • •

    Is Γ\Gamma strictly convex?

  • •

    Is Γ\Gamma regular? (Here, regular means that at every point the supporting plane is unique.)

  • •

    If Γ\Gamma is regular, is it C2C^{2}, or even C∞C^{\infty}?

  • •

    Is Γ\Gamma axially symmetric?

By the arguments in Section 4, one can prove that the minimizing surface Γ\Gamma to Santaló’s problem with area SS is contained in a geodesic ball B⁡(g⁡(S))B(g(S)) for some monotonically increasing function gg such that limS→0+g⁡(S)=0\lim_{S\to 0^{+}}g(S)=0. Hence when SS is small enough, Γ\Gamma also lies in a small neighborhood of a point pp in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3}, and, as S→0+S\to 0^{+}, its geometric quantities can be arbitrarily close to its Euclidean image in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}, under the Beltrami-Klein identity map Id\operatorname{Id} defined in (2.3) (where we take the origin to be pp). Thus we may speculate when the area SS is small enough, the minimizer is close to a geodesic sphere, which is the minimizer to Minkowski Inequality (1.2) in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}.

When SS is large enough, some mechanism we do not fully understand yet causes the flat double disks, whose mean curvature is concentrated entirely on the "edge", to have lower total mean curvature than spheres with the same area, and to become candidates for minimizers to Santaló’s problem. This phenomenon is possibly connected with the exponential growth of geometric quantities in hyperbolic spaces. As r→∞r\to\infty, for a geodesic sphere in ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3}, its area and total mean curvature both grow at the rate of e2​re^{2r}; in contrast, for a geodesic sphere in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}, its area grows at the rate of r2r^{2}, and total mean curvature at the rate of rr. This difference between hyperbolic and Euclidean geometry makes Santaló’s problem more complicated. In view of the family of convex surfaces constructed in Section 4, when the area SS is large, one may speculate that the minimizer has singular points, is therefore non-smooth, and is close to a flat double disk.

Question 5.7.

Let Γ⁡(S)\Gamma(S) be a minimizer to Santaló’s problem with surface area SS. Then

  • •

    If S→0S\to 0, will Γ⁡(S)\Gamma(S), after proper rescaling, converge to a sphere?

  • •

    If S→∞S\to\infty, will Γ⁡(S)\Gamma(S), after proper rescaling, converge to a flat double disk?

Appendix: Computation of Φ1​(Ω⁡(r,α),Γ3​(r,α))\Phi_{1}(\Omega(r,\alpha),\Gamma_{3}(r,\alpha))

In this appendix, we will recall the notion of curvature measures in hyperbolic spaces, and give a detailed computation of Φ1​(Ω⁡(r,α),Γ3​(r,α))\Phi_{1}(\Omega(r,\alpha),\Gamma_{3}(r,\alpha)) defined in Section 4.

Let 𝒦0​(ℍn+1)\mathcal{K}_{0}(\mathbb{H}^{n+1}) be the set of compact convex sets in ℍn+1\mathbb{H}^{n+1} with non-empty interior. For any K∈𝒦0​(ℍn+1)K\in\mathcal{K}_{0}(\mathbb{H}^{n+1}), and ϵ>0\epsilon>0, we define the set

Kϵ\displaystyle K_{\epsilon} =\displaystyle= {x∈ℍn+1:distℍn+1⁡(x,K)≤ϵ}.\displaystyle\{x\in\mathbb{H}^{n+1}:\operatorname{dist}_{\mathbb{H}^{n+1}}(x,K)\leq\epsilon\}.

The map fK:ℍn+1\K→∂Kf_{K}:\mathbb{H}^{n+1}\backslash K\rightarrow\partial K is defined by

(5.12) distℍn+1⁡(fK​(x),x)=distℍn+1⁡(x,K),\displaystyle\operatorname{dist}_{\mathbb{H}^{n+1}}(f_{K}(x),x)=\operatorname{dist}_{\mathbb{H}^{n+1}}(x,K),

and is well-defined because KK is convex. We call fKf_{K} the metric projection onto KK. For β⊂ℍn+1\beta\subset\mathbb{H}^{n+1}, we also define

Mϵ​(K,β):=fK−1​(β∩∂K)∩(Kϵ\K).\displaystyle M_{\epsilon}(K,\beta):=f_{K}^{-1}(\beta\cap\partial K)\cap(K_{\epsilon}\backslash K).

Following Kohlmann [18], Allendoerfer [1], define a Radon measure μϵ\mu_{\epsilon} on the Borel σ\sigma-algebra of hyperbolic space ℬ⁡(ℍn+1)\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{H}^{n+1}) by

μϵ​(K,β)=Volℍn+1⁡(Mϵ​(K,β)),\displaystyle\mu_{\epsilon}(K,\beta)=\operatorname{Vol}_{\mathbb{H}^{n+1}}(M_{\epsilon}(K,\beta)),

Set ln+1−r(t):=∫0tsinhn−r(x)coshr(x)dx,r=0,⋯,nl_{n+1-r}(t):=\int_{0}^{t}\sinh^{n-r}(x)\cosh^{r}(x)dx,r=0,\cdots,n. Then the following Steiner-type formula holds. See [1], [18].

(5.13) μϵ​(K,β)=∑r=0nln+1−r​(ϵ)​Φr​(K,β),∀β∈ℬ⁡(ℍn+1).\mu_{\epsilon}(K,\beta)=\sum_{r=0}^{n}l_{n+1-r}(\epsilon)\Phi_{r}(K,\beta),\qquad\forall\beta\in\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{H}^{n+1}).

When η=∂K∩β\eta=\partial K\cap\beta is a C3C^{3} surface, Φr​(K,⋅)\Phi_{r}(K,\cdot) has the following simple expression:

Φr​(K,β)=∫ησn−rK​(κ)​d​μg,\Phi_{r}(K,\beta)=\int_{\eta}\sigma_{n-r}^{K}(\kappa)d\mu_{g},

where μg\mu_{g} is the surface area measure on ∂K\partial K induced by Volℍn+1\operatorname{Vol}_{\mathbb{H}^{n+1}}. σn−rK\sigma_{n-r}^{K} is the (n−r)(n-r)-th elementary symmetric function of the principal curvatures of ∂K\partial K. Generally, Φn−r​(K,⋅)\Phi_{n-r}(K,\cdot) is called the rr-th curvature measure of the convex body KK. In particular, Φ0​(K,⋅)\Phi_{0}(K,\cdot) is called Gaussian curvature measure, and Φn−1​(K,⋅)\Phi_{n-1}(K,\cdot) is called mean curvature measure. For any convex surface Γ\Gamma in ℍn+1\mathbb{H}^{n+1} with enclosed convex body Ω=conv⁡(Γ)\Omega=\operatorname{conv}(\Gamma), the total mean curvature of Γ\Gamma is given by M⁡(Γ)=Φn−1​(Ω,ℍn+1)=Φn−1​(Ω,Γ)M(\Gamma)=\Phi_{n-1}(\Omega,\mathbb{H}^{n+1})=\Phi_{n-1}(\Omega,\Gamma).

For the convex surface Γ⁡(r,α)⊂ℍ3\Gamma(r,\alpha)\subset\mathbb{H}^{3} defined in Section 4, we will now use (5.13) to compute Φ1​(Ω⁡(r,α),Γ3​(r,α))\Phi_{1}(\Omega(r,\alpha),\Gamma_{3}(r,\alpha)). Since Γ3​(r,α)\Gamma_{3}(r,\alpha) consists of two identical "circular edges", we define

Γ3+(r,α):={x∈Γ3(r,α):Id(x)∈Bℝ3(1)∩{x3>0}},\Gamma_{3}^{+}(r,\alpha):=\left\{x\in\Gamma_{3}(r,\alpha):\operatorname{Id}(x)\in B_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}(1)\cap\{x_{3}>0\}\right\},

where Id\operatorname{Id} is the Beltrami-Klein identity map defined in (2.3). Then it suffices to compute Φ1​(Ω⁡(r,α),Γ3+​(r,α))\Phi_{1}(\Omega(r,\alpha),\Gamma_{3}^{+}(r,\alpha)).

To simplify the computation, we will use polar coordinates to model ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3}. That is, we identify ℍ3\mathbb{H}^{3} with (U,g¯)(U,\bar{g}) by the coordinate isometry Pol:ℍ3→(U,g¯)\operatorname{Pol}:\mathbb{H}^{3}\to(U,\bar{g}), where

U:={(ρ,θ,ϕ):ρ≥0,0≤θ≤π,0≤ϕ<2π},\displaystyle U:=\left\{(\rho,\theta,\phi):\rho\geq 0,0\leq\theta\leq\pi,0\leq\phi<2\pi\right\},

endowed with metric

g¯=d​ρ2+sinh2⁡(ρ)​d​θ2+sinh2⁡(ρ)​sin2⁡(θ)​d​ϕ2.\displaystyle\bar{g}=d\rho^{2}+\sinh^{2}(\rho)d\theta^{2}+\sinh^{2}(\rho)\sin^{2}(\theta)d\phi^{2}.

g¯\bar{g} is well-defined in the subset of UU where ρ>0\rho>0 and 0<θ<π0<\theta<\pi, but can be naturally extended to all of UU. Note that we will choose the origin such that the origin in polar coordinates Pol−1{ρ=0}=A=Id−1(0,0,r^cos(α))\operatorname{Pol}^{-1}\{\rho=0\}=A=\operatorname{Id}^{-1}(0,0,\hat{r}\cos(\alpha)).

Then we can place Γ⁡(r,α)\Gamma(r,\alpha) such that

and

=Pol−1{\displaystyle=\operatorname{Pol}^{-1}\{ (ρ,θ,ϕ)∈U:There exists 0≤γ≤π2−β,0<t<ϵ, such that\displaystyle(\rho,\theta,\phi)\in U:\text{There exists }0\leq\gamma\leq\frac{\pi}{2}-\beta,0<t<\epsilon,\text{ such that }
sinh⁡(t)sin⁡(π2−θ)=sinh⁡(ρ)sin⁡(π2+γ), and\displaystyle\frac{\sinh(t)}{\sin(\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta)}=\frac{\sinh(\rho)}{\sin(\frac{\pi}{2}+\gamma)},\text{ and }
cosh(ρ)=cosh(r1)cosh(t)−sinh(r1)sinh(t)cos(π2+γ)}\displaystyle\cosh(\rho)=\cosh(r_{1})\cosh(t)-\sinh(r_{1})\sinh(t)\cos(\frac{\pi}{2}+\gamma)\}

by the hyperbolic law of cosines and sines. Set

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.
